tier_reason: The README prints the project's own benchmark output (sort run from the old example/bench.cpp, now benchmarks/bench_sort.cpp; merge run from benchmarks/bench_merge.cpp) against std::sort, std::stable_sort and std::inplace_merge, with compiler and -O2 flags stated but no CPU model, so it falls short of A; first-party only, so C.

corrections.workload: bench_sort: 100000-element int vectors (values (i+1)*10) and std::string vectors (their decimal strings), randomized (fixed-seed mt19937 shuffle), reversed or already sorted; each figure is the std::clock CPU time of 100 iterations of copy-then-sort. bench_merge: a 100000-element sequence whose two subranges, split at 19 middle positions, are each sorted before merging; each cell is total milliseconds (steady_clock) for 100 merges, and the reported figure is a trapezoidal average over middle positions. In the merge 'sorted' case the two subranges are already in final order (no overlap), in the 'reversed' case they are non-overlapping but swapped, and in the 'randomized' case they overlap heavily.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README bench_sort output (seconds for 100 sorts of 100000 elements): reversed int std::sort 0.045461 vs timsort 0.019139 (about 2.4x, derived from page data); sorted int 0.021876 vs 0.008042 (about 2.7x, derived from page data); reversed std::string 0.586707 vs 0.345099 (about 1.7x, derived from page data); sorted std::string 0.402458 vs 0.298639 (about 1.35x, derived from page data); against std::stable_sort, reversed int 0.575431 vs 0.019139 (about 30x, derived from page data) and reversed std::string 2.715778 vs 0.345099 (about 7.9x, derived from page data). On randomized data timsort is SLOWER: int std::sort 0.695253 vs timsort 1.255825, std::string 3.438217 vs 5.791845 (also slower than std::stable_sort 0.868916 and 4.122629). README and wiki bench_merge output (ms for 100 merges, averaged over middle positions): sorted std::string std::inplace_merge 158.238114 vs timmerge 0.273858 (about 578x, derived from page data; the subranges are already in order, so timmerge's galloping does almost no work), sorted int 4.291098 vs 0.105571, reversed int 11.441404 vs 4.017482 (about 2.8x), reversed std::string 305.649503 vs 114.773898 (about 2.7x), randomized std::string 324.964249 vs 210.297207 (about 1.5x); randomized int 33.404430 vs 37.047990 (timmerge slower).
corrections.caveats: Tier C: the project's own benchmark code with compiler and flags but no CPU model and no standard-library statement. The README sort output was produced with Apple LLVM 7.0.0 (2015 toolchain, libc++ of that era) at -O2 from the old C++11 example/bench.cpp, not from a run of the current benchmarks directory built with -DBUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON; std::sort implementations have changed since, so current ratios may differ. The README states plainly that timsort is slower than std::ranges::sort on randomized sequences and faster only on partially-sorted ones, so the win is limited to presorted, reversed or nearly sorted inputs. Baseline for the 'faster' rows is std::sort, which is not stable; the fair stable baseline is std::stable_sort (also beaten on reversed and sorted input, also slower on random input). Sort timings are CPU-clock totals for 100 iterations that each include a std::copy of the input, timed on all three algorithms alike. The headline 578x merge figure is the degenerate case where the two runs are already in final order (timmerge gallops past them while std::inplace_merge still does linear work); on heavily overlapping int runs timmerge is slower. The merge run used GCC 10.2.0 on Manjaro x86_64 (wiki https://github.com/timsort/cpp-TimSort/wiki/Benchmark-results lists all middle positions) with no CPU model. The repo moved from gfx/cpp-TimSort to timsort/cpp-TimSort; the old URL redirects. The current 3.x.y branch requires C++20; the 2.x.y (C++11) and 1.x.y (C++03) branches are no longer actively maintained.

notes: All README numbers match the record; bench_sort.cpp and bench_merge.cpp (100 iterations each, merge output checked with is_sorted) look sound, with no correctness or no-op problem found. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: faster only on presorted or reversed input (slower than std::sort and std::stable_sort on random data), no CPU model, sort numbers from a 2015 Apple clang toolchain, and the 578x merge row is a no-overlap degenerate case.
